unit.title: Inception & “Build Just Enough Process”
unit.moc: the 4 core terms — the core principle — what it does/doesn't — the 7-step loop — the name

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint 1 — gate
checkpoint.prompt: Reproduce the 4 core terms and the core principle, and name what the tribunal is NOT. Write a short verdict.

facts.text: **the Living Tribunal** is the whole system for getting one hard question answered by several independent AI models. You open it with a single problem and it closes with a single verdict — a courtroom where the models are witnesses, not the judge.

The four terms exist so anyone can describe a run without ambiguity: `the Living Tribunal` is the system, `A Sitting` is one problem run, `Quorum` is the multi-model vote, `Convergence` is the final verdict. Naming each stage stops people from mixing up 'the vote' with 'the answer'.

In practice the `hub` CLI drives the whole thing: you hand it one brief and it farms that brief out to the lanes, collects their votes, and writes the Convergence. The model is only the engine doing the reasoning inside one lane.
A common slip is calling the model 'the tribunal'. It is not — the model is one lane's engine. The tribunal is the system of lanes, votes, and the converged verdict, run by the `hub` CLI.

exercises.prompt: One problem run through the tribunal is called:
The multi-model vote over that problem is:
Match each term to its meaning.

lessons.title: Core Principle: Build Just Enough Process

facts.text: Formalize Thinly means write down just enough process to keep the discipline — independence, grounding, and a recorded dissent — and no more. The point is the discipline, not a pile of machinery.

Discipline is the product because it survives model swaps. When the process is thin you can change lanes or models without rewriting a bureaucracy; the value is the habit of challenging and citing, not the tooling.

The 'whole system' is just four artifacts: this document, the intake template, the ledger, and the `hub` CLI. There is no hidden server or special environment — if it is not one of those four, it is not the system.

The habit has already paid off: it caught an AI's wrong Cloudflare/Prisma/Neon claims, audited a session report, and shipped a migration blueprint. That is more real validation than most tools ever get.

Players often read 'just enough process' as 'less rigor'. It is not — it means the rigor is enforced by gates, not by a heavy build. The learn checkpoint at the end of this unit is exactly one of those gates.

exercises.prompt: Formalize Thinly means the value is ___ , not the machinery.
Which of these is NOT part of “the whole system”?
The tribunal's habit has already caught a wrong model claim and audited a session report.

lessons.title: What the Tribunal Does (and Doesn't Do)

facts.text: The tribunal takes one problem from any session and returns ONE converged, evidence-cited answer. It is a decision service, not a workshop.

It routes the SAME brief through 2–5 independent lanes and grounds the result in the second brain plus fresh docs, because independence plus grounding is what turns opinion into a verdict you can defend.
A real sitting took a 'should we use X?' question, ran it through blind lanes, and came back with a single answer each lane had to defend with a citation — not a chat log, not a git commit.

It is deliberately NOT a build environment, a chat playground, an agent orchestrator, a replacement for reading primary docs, or a place to park lab data or secrets. Treating it as any of those breaks the contract.

exercises.prompt: Which is a true statement about what the tribunal returns?

options: a way to route the same brief to independent lanes
grounded in the second brain + fresh docs
a build environment that returns commits
a way to force lanes to challenge each other

exercises.prompt: Which statement VIOLATES the tribunal's stated scope?
exercises.scenario: A new team member proposes using the tribunal as a destination for lab data and secrets.
options: grounding the result in the second brain
routing the same brief to independent lanes
storing lab data and secrets with the tribunal

lessons.title: The 7-Step Loop: Intake → Triage → Ground → Route → Converge → Verify → Record

facts.text: Every run walks seven steps: Intake → Triage → Ground → Route → Converge → Verify → Record. Intake is the problem arriving and Record is the verdict filed.
Independence is the product. Each lane sees the SAME brief and no lane sees another's output until convergence — that blindness is what makes the Quorum a real vote instead of groupthink.

In the Verify step you check the artifact the user actually runs: run it, grep the repo, read the vendor doc — never just 'the models agreed'. Record then writes the verdict to the ledger so it stays auditable.

Players sometimes think Route is where lanes 'talk'. It is not — Route is blind dispatch; the lanes only meet at Converge. In the learn path, clearing the unit checkpoint is the Record step made visible.

exercises.prompt: Put the 7 loop steps in order.
What does “verify” mean in the loop?
options: checking against the artifact the user runs

lessons.title: The Name: Quorum — Why It Was Chosen

facts.text: `Quorum` is the name of the hub, chosen to name the one property that makes it work: you need a quorum of independent voices, not a single one.
Real Claude proposed it precisely because it points at independence. A name like `Sounding Board` would have suggested a chat; `Quorum` names a decision rule.
The runner-up was `Crossbench` — another strong name, but it reads as a place rather than a rule. `Quorum` won because it states the mechanism in one word.
A common slip is hearing 'quorum' as a headcount feature of the CLI. It is a principle: the verdict only counts because several independent lanes agreed.

exercises.prompt: Which name was recommended, and why?
options: PolyModel Hub — because it is generic
Quorum — because it names the independence property
Sounding Board — because it is evocative

exercises.prompt: The name “Quorum” was proposed by real Claude.
